title: K-9 Saxon, Oxyglobin & the Saxon Award | Veterinary HBOC
description: Documented 2002 Fresno Police K-9 Saxon trauma case involving Oxyglobin, its historical HBOC record, and the official Saxon Award legacy.
heading: K-9 Saxon: Oxyglobin, survival and the legacy of the Saxon Award.
lead: On 22 August 2002, Fresno Police K-9 Saxon sustained near-fatal shotgun injuries in the line of duty. A contemporaneous letter from Police Chief Jerry Dyer, published in Biopure Corporation's 2002 Annual Report, described Oxyglobin as playing a pivotal role in Saxon's survival. Fresno Police later named the Saxon Award in his honor.

sections.title: A working police dog critically injured in the line of duty.
paragraphs: Biopure's 2002 Annual Report reproduces a letter dated 26 November 2002 from Fresno Police Chief Jerry Dyer. The letter states that Saxon was shot at point-blank range with a shotgun while on duty on 22 August 2002.
The injuries were described as nearly fatal, including lung injury, fractures to two legs and extensive trauma to Saxon's left side.

sections.title: The treatment record is explicit about Oxyglobin.
paragraphs: Chief Dyer wrote that discussions between Fresno Police staff and veterinarian Dr. Roger Gfeller left no doubt, in their view, about the pivotal role Oxyglobin played in saving Saxon's life.

That statement is a contemporaneous testimonial published by Biopure, not a randomized study. Its value is different: it documents real-world emergency use of an FDA-approved veterinary hemoglobin-based oxygen carrier in a named critically injured working dog.

sections.title: Saxon's name became an official Fresno Police award.
paragraphs: The Fresno Police Department policy manual contains Section 1030.5.10, SAXON AWARD. The policy states that the award is given in honor of K-9 Saxon, the first Fresno Police Service Animal to be seriously injured in the line of duty on 22 August 2002.

The award may be given to a police service animal seriously injured in the performance of duty by unlawful force directed at the animal or its handler that could have resulted in death. Saxon's survival therefore left an institutional legacy beyond the original medical event.

sections.title: Real-world evidence of a function: emergency oxygen-carrying support.
paragraphs: Saxon is relevant to the history of veterinary oxygen therapeutics because the case shows Oxyglobin being used outside a controlled trial when a critically injured animal required immediate support.

For modern BHOC research, the historical lesson is not that one case proves a new product. It is that oxygen-delivery therapeutics have a documented veterinary precedent in real-world emergency care. Product identity, formulation, dose, safety, species and indication boundaries must remain explicit.

note: Evidence boundary: the Oxyglobin statement is a historical treatment account published by Biopure and attributed to Fresno Police Chief Jerry Dyer. It is not a controlled efficacy study and does not establish efficacy, safety, approval or endorsement for BHOC.
